exposure: Fecal microbiota composition, specifically Ruminococcus gnavus
outcome: Immune response (cytokines, T-helper cells, eosinophils, mast cells)
cohort: 30 infant twins and 14 age-matched singletons born at National Taiwan University Children's Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan, from April 2011 to March 2013
finding: Increased fecal abundance of Ruminococcus gnavus in early infancy is associated with the development of allergies, particularly respiratory allergies, potentially by modulating the immune response in the gut and lungs.
birth_weight: Recorded, but specific values not mentioned
